courses.title: The Indian monsoon
courses.summary: See how land-sea heating, the Himalayas and the Western Ghats drive India's monsoon rains.
outcomes: Explain how land-sea temperature difference creates monsoon winds
Describe the two branches of the south-west monsoon

steps.title: Land and sea
steps.body: Land heats faster than sea in summer, forming a low over land and high over sea. Air flows from high to low pressure, carrying moisture inland.

steps.title: Importance
steps.body: About 70% of India's annual rainfall comes in the south-west monsoon months (June-September), and agriculture depends on it.

objects.label: Indian peninsula
objects.info: The land that heats quickly in summer. Heated air rises and creates low pressure over north-west India.

objects.label: Arabian Sea
objects.info: Source of moist south-west winds for the west coast. Seas heat more slowly than land.

objects.label: Bay of Bengal
objects.info: The second branch of the monsoon draws moisture from here for eastern and northern India.

objects.label: Himalayas
objects.info: A great barrier that stops the monsoon clouds moving north, forcing rain over the plains, and blocks cold air from Central Asia.

objects.label: Western Ghats
objects.info: Moist winds are forced up the western slopes, cool and drop heavy orographic rain; the eastern side lies in a rain shadow.

objects.label: Thermal low (north-west India)
objects.info: In May-June the Thar region and north-west plains get intensely hot. Rising air creates low pressure that pulls in moist air from the sea.

objects.label: South-west monsoon (Arabian Sea branch)
objects.info: Moist winds bring rain to Kerala around 1 June on average, then move up the west coast.

objects.label: South-west monsoon (Bay branch)
objects.info: Turns west along the Himalayas, bringing rain to eastern and northern India.

objects.label: ITCZ shifts north
objects.info: The Intertropical Convergence Zone, a belt of rising air near the equator, shifts north in summer, helping the monsoon onset.

objects.label: Kerala onset

objects.label: North-east monsoon (winter)

courses.title: Inside a volcano
courses.summary: Slice a volcano in 3D: magma chamber, conduit, vent, crater, lava, ash and layered cone.
outcomes: Name the parts of a volcano
Explain why volcanoes erupt
Contrast shield and stratovolcanoes
Describe hazards and safety

scenes.text: Shake a soda bottle and open it.

steps.title: Magma path
steps.body: Magma collects in a chamber, rises through the conduit and erupts at the vent as lava, gas and ash.

steps.title: India
steps.body: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is India's only confirmed active volcano. The ancient Deccan Traps are a huge lava plateau formed about 66 million years ago.

activity.prompt: Explode the volcano and follow the magma path.

objects.label: Crust and mantle rock
objects.info: Solid rock above the magma. Magma rises because it is less dense than the rock around it.

objects.label: Magma chamber
objects.info: A large reservoir of molten rock a few to tens of kilometres underground. Gas dissolved in the magma drives eruptions.

objects.label: Conduit (main pipe)
objects.info: The channel magma travels up to reach the surface.

objects.label: Volcanic cone
objects.info: Built from layers of lava and ash from past eruptions, so it grows upward over time.

objects.label: Crater and vent
objects.info: The bowl at the summit where magma and gas erupt.

objects.label: Lava flow
objects.info: Magma that reaches the surface is called lava. Basalt lava is runny and can flow for kilometres; sticky lavas pile up near the vent.

objects.label: Ash cloud
objects.info: Fine fragments of rock and glass thrown into the air. Ash can travel hundreds of kilometres, closing airports and harming lungs.

objects.label: Volcanic bombs
objects.info: Blobs of molten rock thrown out during eruption that cool in the air.

objects.label: Dike and side vent
objects.info: Magma can also squeeze through cracks (dikes) and erupt from a side vent.

objects.label: Alternating layers
objects.info: Layers of ash and lava make a stratovolcano. They give the cone its steep, layered structure.

objects.label: Plate boundary
objects.info: Many volcanoes lie where plates collide (subduction) or spread apart, such as the Ring of Fire around the Pacific. Hotspots like Hawaii are another cause.

objects.label: Gas bubbles
objects.info: Dissolved gases (water vapour, CO2, SO2) expand as magma rises, like opening a fizzy drink, driving explosive eruptions.

quiz.q: What is molten rock underground called?
quiz.why: It is called lava once it erupts.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: Shield volcanoes have gentle slopes from runny basalt lava (e.g. Mauna Loa). Stratovolcanoes are steep, layered cones from alternating lava and ash (e.g. Mount Fuji).

steps.title: Largest

steps.title: Surface currents
steps.body: Prevailing winds push surface water. The Coriolis effect (from Earth's rotation) bends flow right in the northern hemisphere and left in the south, producing circular gyres.

steps.title: Speed
steps.body: The Gulf Stream moves at up to about 2 m/s and carries about 30 times the flow of all the world's rivers combined.

steps.title: Doubling rule

objects.label: Sun
objects.info: Our star: a ball of hydrogen and helium about 1.39 million km across. It holds 99.86% of the solar system's mass and fusion in its core makes its light.

objects.label: Mercury
objects.info: Smallest planet and closest to the Sun. It circles the Sun in 88 days, has almost no air, and swings from very hot days to freezing nights.

objects.label: Venus
objects.info: Wrapped in thick carbon-dioxide clouds, with a surface near 465 °C - hotter than Mercury. It spins backwards compared with most planets.

objects.label: Earth
objects.info: The only world known to have life and liquid oceans on its surface. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach it.

objects.label: Mars
objects.info: The red planet, coloured by iron oxide dust. It has Olympus Mons, the tallest known volcano in the solar system (about 22 km high), and two tiny moons.

objects.label: Asteroid belt
objects.info: A region of rocky leftovers between Mars and Jupiter. Despite films, the asteroids are spread very far apart. Ceres, a dwarf planet, lives here.

objects.label: Jupiter
objects.info: The largest planet - over 11 times Earth's width. A gas giant with the Great Red Spot storm and dozens of moons including Io and Europa.

objects.label: Saturn
objects.info: A gas giant famous for bright rings of ice and rock. It is so light for its size that its average density is less than water's.

objects.label: Saturn's rings

objects.label: Uranus
objects.info: An ice giant tipped on its side (axis tilted about 98 degrees). Methane in its air gives a blue-green colour.

objects.label: Neptune
objects.info: The farthest planet, about 30 times Earth's distance from the Sun. It has supersonic winds and takes about 165 years to orbit once.

objects.label: Singularity (idealised)
objects.info: In classical general relativity the mass is squeezed to a point of infinite density. Physicists think new physics (quantum gravity) is needed there.

objects.label: Event horizon
objects.info: The boundary beyond which nothing - not even light - can escape. Its radius for a non-spinning black hole is r = 2GM/c2.

objects.label: Photon sphere
objects.info: At 1.5 times the horizon radius, light can orbit the black hole in unstable circular paths.

objects.label: Accretion disk
objects.info: Hot, glowing gas spiralling in. Friction heats it to millions of degrees so it shines brightly in X-rays.

objects.label: Jet (north)
objects.info: Some black holes launch narrow beams of particles at nearly light speed along the spin axis, powered by magnetic fields.

objects.label: Jet (south)
objects.info: The jet usually appears on both sides of the disk.

objects.label: Companion star
objects.info: In an X-ray binary, a normal star donates gas to the black hole - which is how many stellar-mass black holes are found.

objects.label: Bent light ray
objects.info: Light passing near a massive object follows curved space. Near a black hole this bending (gravitational lensing) is extreme.

steps.title: Shape and colour code
steps.body:
- **Mandatory (regulatory) signs:** circular, mostly red border or blue disc: they give orders (No entry, Speed limit, Compulsory keep left).
- **Cautionary (warning) signs:** triangular with a red border: they warn of hazards (sharp bend, school ahead, slippery road).
- **Informatory signs:** rectangular: they inform (hospital, parking, petrol pump, direction boards).
- Special shapes: **STOP is octagonal**; **Give Way is an inverted triangle**.

steps.title: Core rules
steps.body: In India traffic keeps to the **left**. Overtake on the right when safe, with a clear view and space. At roundabouts give way to traffic already on the roundabout (generally from your right) unless signs say otherwise. Stop at red lights and stop lines; give way to pedestrians at zebra crossings; emergency vehicles with sirens get priority.

steps.title: Never drink and drive
steps.body: Alcohol slows reactions. The legal limit in India is **30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood**, and penalties for exceeding it are serious. Plan a sober driver or a cab.

steps.title: Disclaimer
steps.body: Rules differ by state and change over time. Check the current Motor Vehicles Act rules, your state transport department and the Parivahan portal. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Stopping distance
steps.body: Stopping distance = **thinking distance + braking distance**. Thinking distance = speed × reaction time. At **72 km/h = 20 m/s** and a 1.5 s reaction, thinking distance is **30 m** before the brakes even begin. Braking distance grows with the square of speed; doubling speed roughly quadruples it.

steps.title: Following gap
steps.body: Use the **3-second rule**: when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed mark, you should reach it at least 3 seconds later (more in rain, at night or behind big vehicles).

steps.title: Wet roads
steps.body: Braking distances can be much longer on wet roads; reduce speed and avoid sudden braking.

steps.title: Breakdown

steps.title: Tyre pressure
steps.body: Check pressure with a gauge when tyres are **cold**; use the value on the sticker (door pillar or manual). Low pressure wears edges, heats the tyre and raises fuel use. Check the spare too. Look for cuts, bulges and uneven wear; replace when the tread wear indicators are reached.

steps.title: Change a wheel safely
steps.body:
1. Park on level ground, away from traffic, handbrake on, hazards on, gear in first (or P).
2. Loosen wheel nuts slightly while the wheel is on the ground.
3. Jack the car at the manual's jacking point.
4. Remove nuts and wheel, fit spare, hand-tighten nuts in a star pattern.
5. Lower the car, then tighten fully in a star pattern.
6. Get the pressure and the damaged tyre checked soon.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Never go under a car supported only by a jack. If the location is unsafe, call roadside help.

steps.title: Sort
steps.body: Separate **whites, light colours, dark/new colours**, and delicate items (silk, wool). Check the **care label**: it shows the maximum water temperature, whether to machine wash, and how to dry. When in doubt use cold water.

steps.title: Wash and dry
steps.body: Use detergent as the pack directs (too much leaves residue). Don't overload the machine. Dry dark clothes inside out in shade to prevent fading; whites can dry in sun. Never mix bleach with other cleaners.

steps.title: Chemical safety
steps.body: **Never mix bleach with ammonia or acid cleaners/vinegar**: toxic gases form. Keep detergents away from children.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
Act quickly; blot, don't rub; test on a hidden spot. Typical treatments:
- **Turmeric/curry:** rinse, wash with soap, dry in sunlight (it fades the yellow).
- **Blood:** cold water, never hot (heat sets it).
- **Grease/oil:** dab with dish-wash liquid or sprinkle talc/baking soda to absorb, then wash.
- **Ink:** dab with rubbing alcohol on a cloth from the outside in.
- **Tea/coffee:** cold water rinse then wash.

steps.title: Tools
steps.body: Keep dish soap, rubbing alcohol, baking soda and a soft brush in a stain kit.

steps.title: Never mix

steps.title: MCB trips
steps.body: An MCB trips on overload or a fault. Switch off the appliances, wait, then switch the MCB back on. If it trips again at once, **do not keep resetting**: there may be a short circuit or fault; call a licensed electrician. Never touch wiring with wet hands; switch off the main supply first.

steps.title: Simple fixes
steps.body: **Dripping tap:** close the supply, unscrew the tap head, replace the worn rubber washer. **Blocked sink:** use a plunger or a drain snake before chemical cleaners. **Hanging pictures:** use the right wall plug and check for pipes/wires with a detector.

steps.body: Gas, mains wiring, structural cracks and water-heater faults need qualified help.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: List income. List **needs** (rent, food, transport, bills, EMIs), **wants** (eating out, subscriptions, shopping) and **savings** (emergency fund, investments, insurance). A common guide: **50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings**, adapt it to your situation.

steps.title: Worked example

steps.title: Pay yourself first

steps.title: Emergency fund
steps.body: Aim to build **3–6 months of essential expenses** in an easily accessible account. If essentials are ₹25,000 a month, target ₹75,000–₹1,50,000. Keep health and term insurance as appropriate.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body: Credit-card revolving interest, buy-now-pay-later habits, impulse online buying, loans from unregulated apps, and "guaranteed returns" schemes. Never share OTP, PIN or UPI PIN; the national cyber-crime helpline is **1930**.

steps.title: Not financial advice
steps.body: This is general education, not personalised financial advice.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Open (hook + what you will say), 3 main points with one example each, close (summary + call to action). A talk of 3 minutes is about **400–450 spoken words** at a comfortable pace of ~130–150 words per minute.

steps.title: Hook ideas
steps.body: A question, a short story, a surprising fact. Avoid starting with "Sorry, I'm nervous".

steps.title: Write notes as keywords
steps.body: Do not read a script; use cue cards with key words.

steps.title: Nerves
steps.body: Nerves are normal; they are energy. Slow breathing (in 4, out 6) calms the body. Practise out loud at least three times, stand tall, and look at friendly faces.

steps.title: Voice
steps.body: Speak slightly slower than normal, vary volume, **pause** after key points, and look at different parts of the room. Fill pauses with silence, not "um".

steps.title: Record yourself

- **Position:** what you ask for ("no increase"). **Interest:** why you want it (stable budget, long tenancy).
- Know your **target**, your **walk-away limit** and your **best alternative** if no deal (BATNA: best alternative to a negotiated agreement).

courses.title: Self-defence awareness: prevention, escape and the law
courses.summary: Situational awareness, assertive boundaries, escaping holds in general terms, phone safety tools and the legal right of private defence in general terms.

courses.guardianNote: Covers personal safety and escaping threats, with no graphic content; suitable for older teens with a trusted adult available.

scenes.text: Priya walks from the bus stop to her home.
She notices a man following for two streets.

steps.title: Awareness levels
steps.body: Simple colour code: **white** (unaware, phone-absorbed), **yellow** (relaxed but aware: you scan), **orange** (something feels wrong: plan), **red** (act: leave, shout, call for help). Aim to live in yellow in public.

steps.title: Prevention habits
steps.body: Share location with family on late trips; walk on well-lit, busy routes; keep one earbud out; keep your phone charged; sit near the driver or women's coach; trust your instincts and move toward people, shops, or police if uneasy.

steps.title: Assertive voice
steps.body: Use a firm voice: "Stop. Leave me alone." Loud voice attracts attention. You do not owe politeness to someone who makes you unsafe.

steps.title: Emergency numbers
steps.body: **112** (all emergencies), **181** (women helpline), **1098** (Childline), **1930** (cyber-crime).

a.text: You are walking home at dusk and sense someone following for two streets. What do you do?

choices.label: Cross toward a lit shop, call someone and stay among people
Walk faster into a dark lane

good.text: You reached the shop; the person turned away. If you feel threatened call 112.

bad.text: Head toward people and light; call for help if needed.

lessons.title: Escaping holds and using tools, in general terms

scenes.text: The goal of self-defence is to escape, not to win a fight.
Noise and speed matter.

steps.title: General principles
steps.body: Make noise, create distance, and run to safety. If held by the wrist, rotate your arm toward the gap between the attacker's thumb and fingers (the weakest point) while stepping back; then run. Target soft areas only if needed to break free. Training with a qualified instructor builds real skill; online reading is not a substitute.

steps.title: Tools
steps.body: Learn your phone's emergency SOS feature, share live location, carry a whistle or personal alarm, and use the 112 app/service where available. Practise calling 112 quickly.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: Do not rely on a weapon; it can be taken and used against you, and some items are illegal to carry. Avoid confronting a threat when escape is possible.

steps.title: Right of private defence (general)
steps.body: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, in force from 1 July 2024, every person has a right to defend their own body and property and those of others against certain offences. The force must be **reasonable and proportionate** to the threat, only what is necessary, and the right **ends when the threat ends**. In only certain grave situations may it extend to causing death. Excess force can itself be an offence. Report incidents to the police (112) and speak to a lawyer. This is general education, not legal advice.

For international travel you need a **passport** valid for the period the destination requires (often 6 months), and a **visa** if the destination requires one. courses.summary: What dioxins and PCBs are, why they persist and build up in fat and food chains, how they harm (AhR receptor, cancer, immune, hormone and developmental effects), famous disasters, the Stockholm Convention, and practical ways to cut exposure — especially by not burning waste.

scenes.text: Every winter evening, a pile of plastic and garbage is burnt at the end of Priya's lane.
The thick smoke smells sharp. Her grandmother says, 'It's just rubbish smoke.'
Uncontrolled burning of mixed waste is a major source of dioxins.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: What they are
steps.body: **Dioxins** (polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins and dibenzofurans) are unwanted by-products of **combustion and some industrial processes** — especially burning chlorine-containing waste (PVC plastics) at low temperatures, metal smelting, paper bleaching (older methods). **PCBs** (polychlorinated biphenyls) were deliberately made for electrical transformers, capacitors and other uses until bans from the 1970s onward. The most toxic dioxin is **2,3,7,8-TCDD**, classified by IARC as a known human carcinogen.

steps.title: Persistent, bioaccumulative, toxic
steps.body:
- **Persistent:** they resist breakdown for years in soil and sediment
- **Fat-loving (lipophilic):** they store in body fat — the half-life of dioxins in the human body is estimated at about **7–11 years**
- **Biomagnification:** concentrations rise up food chains: plankton → small fish → big fish → humans
WHO estimates that **over 90% of human exposure is through food**, mainly meat, dairy, fish and shellfish.

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body: Dioxins and dioxin-like PCBs bind the **aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR)** inside cells, switching on genes that alter cell growth, hormone and immune function. Effects: **chloracne** (severe acne-like skin lesions) after high exposure; reproductive and developmental problems; immune suppression; hormone disruption; and cancer.

lessons.title: How lead harms the body

scenes.text: Arjun, 6, lives beside an informal battery-recycling yard. He is pale, irritable and struggles at school.

Lead damage to a developing brain is often silent — and lasting.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body: Lead **mimics calcium** and zinc, entering cells and interfering with nerve signalling, enzymes and bone. It **inhibits haem synthesis** (ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase) → **anaemia**. It crosses the placenta and the developing **blood–brain barrier**. Most body lead ends up stored in **bone**, from where it can be released later (e.g. in pregnancy).

steps.title: Effects
steps.body:
- **Children:** reduced IQ and attention, learning and behaviour problems, slowed growth, anaemia, hearing problems; very high levels → abdominal pain, seizures, coma
- **Adults:** high BP, kidney damage, anaemia, nerve damage (wrist drop), reproductive harm, miscarriage risk
WHO states **there is no level of lead exposure known to be without harmful effects**. A 2020 UNICEF–Pure Earth report estimated around **800 million children** worldwide have blood lead at or above 5 µg/dL.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Dry-sweeping dusty floors

- Buying unusually bright loose turmeric

steps.title: Testing
steps.body: Diagnosis is by **blood lead level (BLL)**, in µg/dL. The US CDC uses a **blood lead reference value of 3.5 µg/dL** (2021) to identify children with higher exposure than most. Doctors also check haemoglobin and iron.

steps.title: Treatment

1. **Find and remove the source** — the most important step
2. Nutrition: adequate **iron, calcium** and vitamin C reduce lead absorption
3. At high levels doctors may use **chelation therapy** (e.g. succimer, CaNa2EDTA) — only under specialist supervision; never use unregulated 'detox' products
4. Developmental follow-up for children

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice

steps.title: Forms
steps.body:
- **Elemental (metallic) mercury:** thermometers, BP machines, CFLs, dental amalgam, artisanal gold mining. Swallowed, it is poorly absorbed; **inhaled vapour** is well absorbed → nervous system, lungs, kidneys
- **Inorganic mercury salts:** some skin-lightening creams, older antiseptics; damage kidneys and gut
- **Organic methylmercury:** formed by microbes in water; builds up in fish; most dangerous to the **developing brain**

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body: Mercury binds strongly to **sulfhydryl (–SH) groups** on proteins and enzymes, disrupting cell function. Methylmercury crosses the blood–brain barrier and placenta. Symptoms of high exposure: tremor, irritability, memory problems, numbness, vision and hearing loss, kidney damage.

steps.title: Common mistakes

His family has drunk from the same clear, sweet-tasting hand-pump for 20 years.
A field test shows high arsenic.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Where it comes from
steps.body: Arsenic is **geogenic** — released naturally from sediments into groundwater under certain chemical conditions. In India, high levels are found in parts of the Ganga–Brahmaputra plains (e.g. West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Assam, Jharkhand) and some other areas. It is **colourless, odourless and tasteless**. WHO has called arsenic contamination in Bangladesh the largest mass poisoning of a population in history.

steps.title: Mechanism and effects
steps.body: Inorganic arsenic (especially arsenite, As(III)) binds sulfhydryl groups and disrupts cellular energy production; arsenate mimics phosphate. Long-term exposure (**arsenicosis**) causes skin pigmentation changes, **keratosis** of palms and soles, cancers of **skin, bladder and lung** (IARC Group 1), heart disease, diabetes, nerve damage, and effects on child development.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: **WHO guideline: 10 µg/L** (0.01 mg/L). India's drinking-water standard **BIS IS 10500: 0.01 mg/L** with no relaxation.

lessons.title: Lab: Fluoride — good teeth, bad bones

scenes.text: Children in a dry district have brown-stained, pitted teeth.
Some adults have stiff spines and bent legs — skeletal fluorosis.

steps.title: Too little vs too much
steps.body: Low fluoride (around 0.5–1 mg/L) helps prevent tooth decay. But high fluoride in groundwater — common in parts of **Rajasthan, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh** and others — causes **fluorosis**.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: WHO guideline **1.5 mg/L**. BIS IS 10500: **acceptable 1.0 mg/L**, **permissible 1.5 mg/L** (in the absence of an alternative source).

steps.title: Effects
steps.body:
- **Dental fluorosis** (children during tooth formation): white streaks → brown stains and pitting; permanent
- **Skeletal fluorosis** (long-term high intake): joint pain, stiffness, bone deformities, calcified ligaments
- Non-skeletal effects reported at high levels
India runs a **National Programme for Prevention and Control of Fluorosis (NPPCF)**.

steps.body:
- Judging water safety by taste or clarity
- Boiling to remove arsenic or fluoride (it concentrates them)

scenes.text: Suresh sprays an insecticide on cotton all morning in the heat, without gloves or a mask.
By afternoon he is sweating, drooling, vomiting, with blurred vision and twitching muscles.
This is organophosphate poisoning — a medical emergency.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor. In an emergency call 112. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, call Tele-MANAS 14416.

steps.title: Organophosphates and carbamates
steps.body:
They **inhibit acetylcholinesterase (AChE)**, the enzyme that breaks down the nerve messenger **acetylcholine**. ACh builds up at nerve endings → over-stimulation:
- **Muscarinic:** sweating, salivation, tears, urination, diarrhoea, vomiting, **pinpoint pupils**, slow heart, **bronchorrhoea** (lungs fill with secretions), wheeze
- **Nicotinic:** muscle twitching, weakness, paralysis (including breathing muscles)
- **Brain:** confusion, seizures, coma
Death is usually from **respiratory failure**.

steps.title: Other dangerous agents
steps.body:
- **Paraquat** (herbicide): no antidote; causes lung fibrosis and multi-organ failure even after small amounts
- **Aluminium phosphide** (grain fumigant tablets): releases **phosphine** gas; very high fatality; causes shock
- **Organochlorines** (e.g. DDT, endosulfan — endosulfan banned in India by the Supreme Court in 2011 after harm in Kasaragod): persistent, nerve-excitatory

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Spraying without gloves, mask or long sleeves
- Storing pesticide in drink bottles or kitchens
- Inducing vomiting or giving milk after poisoning
- Dismissing someone who talks about self-harm

scenes.text: You find Suresh collapsed near the spray tank, vomiting, clothes soaked with pesticide.

steps.title: First aid
steps.body:
1. **Protect yourself** (gloves if possible; avoid contact with vomit and spray)
2. **Call 112** — hospital treatment (atropine, oxygen, ventilation, other drugs) is urgent
3. Move to fresh air/shade; **remove contaminated clothes**; wash skin with soap and plenty of water; rinse eyes
4. If unconscious but breathing: **recovery position**; if not breathing — call for help; mouth-to-mouth is risky with pesticide on the face (use a barrier or hands-only CPR as trained)
5. **Do not induce vomiting**; don't give milk, oil or 'home remedies'
6. Take the **pesticide container/label** to hospital

steps.title: In hospital
steps.body: **Atropine** blocks muscarinic effects and dries the lungs; oxygen and ventilation support breathing; **oximes** (pralidoxime) are used in some protocols. Patients may need ICU care and can deteriorate later (intermediate syndrome).

steps.title: Safe use

- **PPE:** gloves, mask/respirator, goggles, long sleeves, boots
- Don't spray against the wind, in peak heat, or eat/drink/smoke while spraying
- Wash body and clothes separately afterwards
- Respect **pre-harvest intervals**

steps.title: Storage and disposal
steps.body: Lock pesticides away from homes, food and children; **never** store in food or drink bottles; never reuse empty containers for water or food — triple-rinse and dispose as instructed.

steps.title: Residues on food
steps.body: Wash fruit and vegetables under running water; peeling and cooking reduce some residues. FSSAI sets maximum residue limits (MRLs).

scenes.text: Aarav opens an old trunk in the attic and a cloud of dust rises.
Three sneezes in a row! He wonders who decided his nose should do that.
His nose did not decide. A reflex did, in a split second, without asking him.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: The reflex arc
steps.body: Irritants such as dust, pollen or a cold virus stimulate nerve endings in the nasal lining. Signals travel along the **trigeminal nerve** to a sneeze-coordinating region in the brainstem. The brainstem then triggers a coordinated burst: a deep breath, closing of the glottis, a sudden squeeze by chest and abdominal muscles, then a rapid release of air through nose and mouth.

steps.title: Purpose
steps.body: A sneeze clears irritants and mucus from the nasal passages. It also sprays droplets, so catching it in a tissue or your elbow protects others.

steps.title: The photic sneeze reflex
steps.body: Some people sneeze when they step into bright light (also called ACHOO syndrome). It runs in families. A popular explanation is crossed wiring between the optic nerve and the trigeminal nerve, but the exact mechanism is still debated.

steps.title: Do not hold it in
steps.body: Pinching the nose and shutting the mouth to stop a sneeze raises pressure in the airways. Rare injuries have been reported. It is better to let it out into a tissue.

steps.title: Experiment idea
steps.body: Ask family members whether bright light makes them sneeze. Do not stare at the sun. Walk from a dim room to a bright doorway and note who sneezes.

statements.s: If you keep your eyes open while sneezing, they can pop out.
statements.why: Eye sockets hold the eyeball firmly. Eyes close by reflex but nothing would pop out.

statements.s: Sneezing is an involuntary reflex coordinated by the brainstem.
statements.why: Once triggered it is largely automatic.

statements.s: Your heart stops for a moment during a sneeze.
statements.why: Chest pressure can briefly change heart rhythm slightly, but the heart does not stop.

statements.s: Some people sneeze in bright light.
statements.why: This is the photic sneeze reflex.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice

steps.title: What a hiccup is
steps.body: A hiccup is a sudden involuntary contraction of the **diaphragm** (the dome-shaped breathing muscle). A split second later the vocal cords snap shut, which makes the 'hic' sound as air is cut off.

steps.title: The reflex loop
steps.body: Signals travel along the phrenic and vagus nerves to the brainstem and back. Common triggers are eating fast, fizzy drinks, alcohol, sudden temperature change of food, and excitement.

steps.title: Before birth
steps.body: Babies hiccup in the womb, so hiccups start long before they have anything to eat. Why we have them is not settled; some scientists suggest an old reflex linked to early breathing practice.

steps.title: Home methods
steps.body: Holding your breath briefly or sipping cold water may help because they change breathing pattern and CO2 or stimulate the vagus nerve. Evidence is mostly anecdotal but they are harmless.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: Most hiccups stop within minutes to hours. Hiccups lasting more than 48 hours, or that stop you eating, sleeping or breathing normally, need a medical check.

statements.why: Followed by sudden closure of the vocal cords.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Not just sleepiness
steps.body: People yawn when tired, bored, and also around transitions such as waking up. Animals yawn too. The honest answer is that the purpose of yawning is not fully settled.

steps.title: Brain cooling hypothesis
steps.body: One leading idea is that a deep yawn increases blood flow and draws in cooler air, helping regulate brain temperature. Some studies link yawn frequency to temperature, but the idea is still being tested.

steps.title: A debunked idea
steps.body: The belief that yawning brings in extra oxygen because blood oxygen is low was tested. People breathing air with more oxygen or more CO2 did not yawn less or more, so this explanation is not supported.

steps.title: Contagious yawns
steps.body: Seeing, hearing or even reading about a yawn can trigger one. This tends to appear in childhood. Links to empathy and social bonding have been proposed but the evidence is mixed.

steps.title: Experiment
steps.body: Count your own yawns over a day in a diary, and note room temperature and time. Look for patterns.

statements.why: Experiments with oxygen-rich air did not change yawning.

scenes.text: Riya hears a spooky story on a cold night.
The hairs on her arms stand up and her cheeks go warm.
At the sad ending of the film she cries. All three are the body talking.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Goosebumps
steps.body: Tiny muscles (**arrector pili**) at each hair root contract when the sympathetic nervous system fires, pulling the hair upright. In furry animals this traps warm air or makes them look bigger. In humans with little body hair, the effect is mostly a leftover.

steps.title: Blushing
steps.body: Emotions such as embarrassment activate the sympathetic system and widen blood vessels in the face and neck, so more blood flows near the skin. Darwin called blushing the most peculiar and most human of expressions.

steps.title: Three kinds of tears
steps.body: Basal tears keep the eye moist, reflex tears wash out irritants such as onion fumes, and emotional tears come with strong feelings. Emotional crying is controlled by the autonomic nervous system and the brain's emotional centres.

steps.title: Myth alert
steps.body: The idea that crying flushes out toxins is not supported by good evidence. Many people say they feel calmer after crying, especially with support from others.

steps.title: Try
steps.body: Observe goosebumps when you step into a cold breeze or hear a favourite piece of music. Note both triggers.

statements.s: Goosebumps are caused by tiny muscles at hair roots.
statements.why: Arrector pili muscles pull hairs upright.

statements.s: Blushing happens because blood vessels in the face widen.
statements.why: More blood flows near the skin.

statements.s: Crying removes toxins from the body.
statements.why: This claim lacks good scientific support.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: What a cramp is
steps.body: A cramp is a sudden, involuntary, painful contraction of a muscle that does not relax straight away. Calf, foot and thigh muscles are common.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body: Overuse and fatigue, muscles held in a shortened position, and nerve over-excitability are the main ideas. The common belief that cramps are caused by dehydration or low salts is less well supported by studies than people think, though heat cramps in people working long hours in hot conditions are real.

steps.title: First aid
steps.body: Gently stretch the muscle and massage it. For a calf cramp, pull the foot upwards towards the shin and walk a little.

steps.title: See a doctor if
steps.body: Cramps are frequent, severe, come with swelling or redness of one leg, weakness, or begin after starting a new medicine.

steps.title: Prevention
steps.body: Regular gentle stretching and gradual increase in exercise help many people.

statements.s: A cramp is an involuntary muscle contraction.
statements.why: The muscle contracts and does not relax quickly.

statements.s: Gentle stretching can relieve a cramp.
Bananas are proven to prevent all cramps.
statements.why: No strong evidence supports a single food cure.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Brain freeze
steps.body: Rapid cooling of the palate is thought to cause quick constriction and then widening of blood vessels, with pain felt in the forehead through shared trigeminal nerve pathways. It is called referred pain. It usually passes within a minute or so.

steps.title: Fix

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: The chemistry
steps.body: Cutting an onion breaks cells so an enzyme (alliinase) meets sulfur compounds. They form sulfenic acids, then another enzyme (lachrymatory factor synthase) converts them into **syn-propanethial-S-oxide**, a volatile gas.

steps.title: The tears
steps.body: The gas reaches the eye and activates nerve receptors on the cornea, so the brain triggers reflex tears to wash it away.

steps.title: Reduce tears
steps.body: Chill the onion first, use a very sharp knife (less cell damage), or cut under a fan so the gas blows away. Evidence for a flame or bread in the mouth is weak.

steps.title: Goggles
steps.body: Sealed swim goggles block gas from the eyes; the tears stop because there is no stimulus.

steps.title: Experiment
steps.body: Compare chopping a room-temperature and a chilled onion, one after another, and rate eye irritation 1–5.

statements.s: Onion tears are caused by a gas released when cells are cut.
A sharper knife can reduce tears.
statements.why: Less cell crushing releases less gas.

statements.s: Only a flame near the onion proves to stop tears.
Onion tears are crying from sadness.

options: Slower enzyme reactions and less volatile gas

steps.title: Capsaicin
steps.body: Chillies contain **capsaicin**, which binds to the receptor TRPV1 on pain nerves. TRPV1 normally detects heat above about 43 °C, so the brain gets a burn signal even though no actual heat damage occurs.

steps.title: Sweating
steps.body: The brain responds as if the mouth is hot: sweating, flushed face, runny nose.

steps.title: Relief
steps.body: Capsaicin dissolves in fat and alcohol, not well in water. Milk, curd or ghee help; casein protein in dairy helps lift capsaicin. Sugar and starch such as rice or bread also give some relief; water mostly spreads it.

steps.title: Why birds eat chillies
steps.body: Birds lack the sensitivity to capsaicin and spread the seeds.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Wash hands after chopping chillies and do not touch eyes. Very high doses can cause stomach pain.

statements.s: Chilli burn is a real heat injury.
statements.why: It is a chemical signal via TRPV1.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice

steps.title: Casein
steps.body: Most milk protein is **casein**, held as tiny micelles that repel each other because of their surface charge, so they stay dispersed.

steps.title: Acid and heat
steps.body: Adding acid (lemon juice, vinegar) lowers pH until casein charges are neutralised near pH 4.6, so micelles clump into curds. Heat speeds up clumping. The liquid left is whey.

steps.title: Other ways
steps.body: Rennet enzyme is used for many cheeses; bacteria that make lactic acid turn milk into curd (dahi).

steps.title: Spoiled milk
steps.body: Milk souring from bacteria growth is unsafe if smelly or unrefrigerated. Curdling in a recipe, with fresh milk and acid, is controlled.

steps.title: Experiment
steps.body: Warm fresh milk, add a spoon of lemon juice at a time and note when curds form.

statements.s: Curdling in paneer-making is controlled protein clumping.
statements.why: Acid neutralises the casein surface charge.

statements.s: Whey is the solid part.
statements.why: Whey is the liquid; curds are solids.

statements.s: Heat speeds curdling.

steps.title: The path
steps.body: Mouth (chewing, salivary amylase starts starch) → oesophagus (peristalsis) → stomach (acid and pepsin, mixing) → small intestine (most digestion and absorption with bile and pancreatic enzymes) → large intestine (water absorption, gut bacteria) → rectum.

steps.title: Length
steps.body: The whole digestive tract is roughly 9 metres long in adults, most of it small intestine.

steps.title: Absorption
steps.body: Villi and microvilli give the small intestine a very large surface area for absorbing nutrients into blood.

steps.title: See a doctor

steps.title: Burping
steps.body: Swallowed air and carbonated gas collect in the stomach; the stomach stretches and the valve at the top relaxes to release it as a burp. Eating fast and fizzy drinks add air.

steps.title: Flatulence
steps.body: Gut bacteria in the large intestine ferment carbohydrates we cannot digest (such as some fibre in beans and lentils), producing gases such as hydrogen, carbon dioxide and sometimes methane. Passing gas many times a day is normal.

steps.title: Smell
steps.body: The smell comes from small amounts of sulfur-containing gases.

steps.title: Reduce
steps.body: Eat slowly, soak and cook pulses well, and increase fibre gradually.

steps.title: The myth
steps.body: Double-blind trials giving children sugar or a sugar-free placebo found no effect on behaviour, even when parents were told their child had sugar. Excitement, party settings and expectations explain the 'rush'.

steps.title: Blood sugar
steps.body: Eating carbohydrates raises blood glucose, and insulin moves glucose into cells. Large sugary meals can be followed by a dip in energy for some people; this is different from hyperactivity.

steps.title: Cravings
steps.body: Cravings come from habit, emotion, stress, poor sleep, and hormones such as ghrelin (hunger) and leptin (fullness). They are not reliably a sign of a specific nutrient shortage.

steps.title: Manage
steps.body: Eat regular balanced meals with protein and fibre, sleep enough, and wait 15 minutes before giving in.

steps.title: Health

scenes.text: Tiya asks her uncle why the sky is blue and not violet.
He says sunlight meets air on its way down.

steps.title: Sunlight is mixed
steps.body: White sunlight contains all colours. Air molecules are much smaller than the wavelength of light, so they scatter light by **Rayleigh scattering**, with strength proportional to 1/λ⁴.

steps.title: Numbers
steps.body: Blue light at about 450 nm is scattered roughly (700/450)⁴ ≈ 5.9 times more than red at 700 nm.

steps.title: Why not violet?
steps.body: Violet scatters even more, but the Sun emits less violet, some is absorbed in the upper atmosphere, and our eyes are less sensitive to violet. The mix looks sky blue.

steps.title: Mars and Moon
steps.body: The Moon has no atmosphere, so its sky is black even in daytime.

steps.title: Never
steps.body: Do not look directly at the Sun.

steps.title: Longer path
steps.body: At sunset sunlight travels through much more atmosphere. Blue and green are scattered out of the beam, leaving orange and red to reach your eyes.

steps.title: Dust and haze
steps.body: Smoke, dust and aerosols add scatter; vivid sunsets are often seen after dust or pollution events, though polluted air is not healthy.

steps.title: Same Sun
steps.body: The Sun is not changing; only the viewing geometry changes.

steps.title: Photography

steps.title: Three steps
steps.body: Sunlight enters a raindrop and **refracts**; different colours bend by slightly different amounts (**dispersion**); it reflects off the back of the drop (internal reflection) and refracts again leaving the drop.

steps.title: Geometry
steps.body: Red emerges at about 42° from the line pointing away from the Sun (the antisolar point), violet at about 40°. So you see a circle's arc with red outside and violet inside. You need the Sun behind you and rain in front.

steps.title: Double and full circles
steps.body: A faint secondary bow appears outside with reversed colours. From a plane you can see a full circle.

steps.title: Myth
steps.body: There is no pot of gold; a rainbow is not an object in a place and each person sees their own.

steps.title: Charge separation
steps.body: In a thundercloud, collisions among ice crystals, graupel and water droplets separate electric charge: typically positive charge higher, negative in the lower part. A huge voltage builds up until air breaks down and a spark jumps.

steps.title: Thunder
steps.body: The channel heats to around 30,000 K almost instantly; the air expands explosively and creates a shock wave we hear as thunder.

steps.title: Distance
steps.body: Sound travels about 343 m/s, so about 3 s per km. 6 seconds between flash and bang means about 2 km.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Go indoors or into a hard-topped vehicle; avoid open fields, tall trees and water; stay away from plumbing and wired devices. If you can hear thunder, you are in range.

steps.title: Fact
steps.body: Lightning rods give lightning a safe path to ground.

scenes.text: Kerala wakes to the first monsoon rain in early June.
Winds now blow from the south-west.

steps.title: Why it happens
steps.body: In summer the Indian land mass heats faster than the Indian Ocean. Warm air rises over land creating low pressure; moist air flows in from the cooler ocean. This seasonal reversal of wind direction is the monsoon (from Arabic mausim, season).

steps.title: Rain
steps.body: Moist air rises over land and mountains such as the Western Ghats, cools, condenses and falls as rain. The Himalayas also stop the air and deflect it.

steps.title: Onset
steps.body: The south-west monsoon typically reaches Kerala around 1 June and covers India by about mid-July; it retreats from late September.

steps.title: Other factors
steps.body: The Coriolis effect, the shifting tropical convergence zone and ocean patterns such as El Niño and the Indian Ocean Dipole influence strength.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Farming, water supply and power demand depend on monsoon rainfall.

statements.s: The monsoon is a seasonal change in wind direction.

The monsoon is just a single big storm.

steps.title: Tides
steps.body: The Moon's gravity pulls more strongly on the near side of Earth than on the far side, which stretches the ocean into two bulges. As Earth spins you pass through two highs and two lows, about every 12 h 25 min, in many places. The Sun adds a smaller effect.

steps.title: Spring and neap
steps.body: At new and full moon, the Sun and Moon line up and spring tides are largest. At quarter moons, neap tides are smaller.

steps.title: Seasons
steps.body: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4°. When your hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, sunlight strikes more directly and days are longer, so it is warmer.

steps.title: Distance myth
steps.body: Earth is closest to the Sun (perihelion) in early January, during northern winter.

steps.title: Why leaves change colour
steps.body: In autumn trees stop making green chlorophyll, revealing yellow and orange carotenoids. Red anthocyanins are newly made in some leaves. Cooler nights and shorter days trigger the change.
